present.explain: A Portuguese verb's ending says who does it: eu tomo (I drink), você toma (you drink), ele or ela toma (he or she drinks), nós tomamos (we drink). você takes the same form as ele and ela. Some common verbs change more: eu tenho, você tem; eu venho, ela vem.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she; Portuguese changes it for who does it, so [[eu tomo]] and [[nós tomamos]] each have their own ending.

examples.literal: I drink coffee.
You drink tea.

examples.means: She drinks a lot of water.
examples.literal: She drinks a lot of water.
We drink water.

contrasts.says: você takes ele's form: você toma, você está.
English adds -s only for he and she; Portuguese has an ending for each person.

mistakes.why: With eu, the verb ends in -o.
With nós, it ends in -mos.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Portuguese noun is an o word or an a word: o celular, o carro; a mesa, a chave. The words with it follow: um café but uma água; meu livro but minha chave; bom and boa. Many a words end in -a and many o words in -o, but not all (a chave, o leite), so learn each noun with its o or a.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the words around it follow: [[o]] celular, [[a]] mesa, and a phone is no more masculine than a table.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The key is in the pocket.
examples.literal: The key is in the pocket.

examples.text: Um chá e uma água, por favor.
examples.means: A tea and a water, please.
examples.literal: A tea and a water, please.

contrasts.says: English has one the and one a; Portuguese has o or a, um or uma, by the noun.
meu and minha follow the noun the same way: meu carro, minha chave.

mistakes.why: celular is an o word.
água is an a word.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: meu (my) goes with an o word and minha with an a word: meu celular, minha chave. seu and sua (your, to someone you say você to) work the same way: seu pai, sua mãe. Brazilians often put o or a in front too: o meu carro, a minha casa; both are right.
possessive.why: my and your follow the thing owned, not the owner: a woman says [[meu]] carro, and a man says [[minha]] chave.

examples.literal: Where is my key?

examples.means: My phone is in my pocket.
examples.literal: My phone is in the pocket.
That is your father?

contrasts.says: meu goes with o words and minha with a words, as o and a do.

mistakes.why: chave is an a word: minha.
pai is an o word: seu.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: não goes right before the verb: Eu não tomo café, Ela não está em casa, Eu não posso ler. With two verbs it goes before the first. English adds do or does (I don't drink); Portuguese only puts não in front.
negation.why: English needs a helper to say not; Portuguese puts [[não]] before the verb itself: Eu [[não]] tomo café, I not drink coffee.

examples.literal: I not drink coffee.

examples.text: Minha mãe não está em casa.
examples.literal: My mother not is at home.

examples.text: Eu não posso ler o livro.
examples.literal: I not can read the book.

contrasts.says: English says don't or isn't; Portuguese says não before the verb.

mistakes.why: não goes before the verb.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes-or-no question keeps a statement's order, and your voice goes up at the end: Você está pronto? (you are ready?), O carro está aqui? A question word goes first: Onde está o carro?, O que você quer? There's no do and no turning words around.
question.why: English turns the words around or adds do; Portuguese asks with the voice: [[Você está]] pronto? is you are ready?

examples.literal: You are ready?
Where is the car?
You want coffee too?

contrasts.says: English puts is or do first; Portuguese keeps the order and lets the voice ask.

mistakes.why: A Brazilian question keeps the statement's order.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

ser-estar.explain: Portuguese has two verbs for to be. ser says what something is: Isso é um livro, O livro é bom. estar says where something is or how it is now: O celular está na mesa, Você está bem?, O café está pronto. Where a thing is takes estar; what it is takes ser.
ser-estar.why: English uses be for both; Portuguese splits it: Isso [[é]] minha chave (what it is), but A chave [[está]] na mesa (where it is).

examples.literal: That is a book.

examples.means: The book is on the table.
examples.literal: The book is on the table.
The tea is ready.

examples.text: O livro é bom e está na mesa.
examples.means: The book is good, and it's on the table.
examples.literal: The book is good and is on the table.

contrasts.says: English has one be; Portuguese chooses ser for what, estar for where and how.

mistakes.why: Where a thing is takes estar.
What something is takes ser.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

voce.explain: Brazilians say você for you, to anyone they'd talk to plainly: friends, family, people their age, most people. Its verb is the same as ele's and ela's: você toma, você está, você quer. For someone older or more formal, there's o senhor and a senhora.
voce.why: English you takes are; Portuguese [[você]] takes the he form: [[você está]], like ele está.

examples.literal: You drinks coffee.
You is well?

examples.means: Do you want to eat here?
examples.literal: You wants eat here?

contrasts.says: você takes ele's form: você toma, ele toma.
o senhor and a senhora are the polite you, with the same verb.

mistakes.why: With você, the ele form: toma.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

modal.explain: After querer (want), poder (can) and precisar (need, have to), the next verb stays in its basic form, ending in -r: Eu quero comer, Você pode ler isso?, Eu preciso trabalhar. Only the first verb changes for who does it, and nothing goes between them: no word for to.
modal.why: [[Eu quero]] already says I want, so the next verb stays plain: [[quero comer]], I want eat.

examples.literal: I want drink coffee.
You can read that?
I still need work.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the form for who (quero, quer, queremos); the second never does.
English puts to between them (want to eat); Portuguese puts nothing.

mistakes.why: After quero, the basic form ending in -r.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

contraction.explain: em (in, on) and de (of) run into o and a after them: em + o is no, em + a is na, de + o is do, de + a is da. So: no bolso (in the pocket), na mesa (on the table), a chave do carro (the key of the car), o livro da minha mãe. They're never written apart.
contraction.why: Portuguese runs the little words together: [[na]] mesa is em a mesa, on the table, said and written as one word.

examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: The key is in the pocket.
examples.literal: The key is in the pocket.

examples.text: Ele tem a chave do meu carro?
examples.means: Does he have the key to my car?
examples.literal: He has the key of the my car?

contrasts.says: no and do go with o words, na and da with a words.

mistakes.wrong: O celular está em a mesa.
mistakes.why: em and a always run together: na.
bolso is an o word: no.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

de.explain: Portuguese has no 's. It joins two nouns with de, in the other order: o livro da minha mãe (the book of my mother: my mother's book). de runs into o and a as do and da. Whose? is De quem?
de.why: English says my mother's book; Portuguese turns it round: o livro [[da]] minha mãe, the book of the my mother.

examples.text: Isso é o livro da minha mãe.
examples.literal: That is the book of the my mother.
Of whom is that phone?

contrasts.says: de and o make do; de and a make da.
English uses 's; Portuguese uses de.

mistakes.right: Isso é o livro da minha mãe.
mistakes.why: Portuguese has no 's: the book of my mother.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: esse goes with an o word and essa with an a word, for this or that: esse livro, essa chave. In Brazil esse is used for this as well as that. On its own, pointing at a thing, it's isso: O que é isso?, Isso é um livro.
demonstrative.why: esse matches the noun like o and a: [[esse]] livro, [[essa]] chave; with no noun, [[isso]].

examples.literal: I read this book.

examples.text: Essa chave é para a senhora.
examples.literal: This key is for the lady.
What is that?

contrasts.says: esse with o words, essa with a words, the way o and a go.

mistakes.why: livro is an o word: esse.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

o-senhor.explain: o senhor (to a man) and a senhora (to a woman) are the polite you: for someone older, a customer, or anyone you'd be formal with. Their verb is ele's, the same as with você: O senhor sabe?, A senhora quer um café? After para, they stay as they are: para o senhor.
o-senhor.why: Portuguese shows respect by calling someone the gentleman or the lady: [[o senhor]] quer um café?, does the gentleman want a coffee?

examples.text: O senhor sabe onde está meu carro?
examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: The gentleman knows where is my car?

examples.text: A senhora quer café com leite?
examples.means: Do you want coffee with milk?
examples.literal: The lady wants coffee with milk?

examples.text: Esse livro é para o senhor.
examples.literal: This book is for the gentleman.

contrasts.says: você for most people; o senhor and a senhora for someone older or formal. Both take ele's verb.
English has one you; Portuguese says você or o senhor by who you're talking to.

mistakes.why: With o senhor, the ele form: sabe.

mistakes.wrong: Essa chave é para o senhora.
mistakes.right: Essa chave é para a senhora.
mistakes.why: a senhora, for a woman.

source.note: Written with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

tem.explain: In everyday Brazil, tem can introduce someone or something that is there: Tem alguém na porta. It has no personal subject in this use. The same tem is also the verb with ele, ela or você when someone has something. Existential tem is used for both one and more than one; formal writing often uses há.
tem.why: [[Tem]] alguém na porta says someone is there. English supplies [[there is]]; Portuguese needs no word for there here.

examples.literal: Has someone at the door.
Has a door open.

contrasts.says: Eu tenho is I have. In Tem alguém na porta, tem introduces someone who is there.
English says there is or there are; everyday Brazilian Portuguese can use tem for either.

mistakes.why: The noun after tem still takes its own article: porta is feminine, so uma.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: An adjective describing a noun often comes after it: uma porta aberta, an open door. It also agrees with that noun: aberto for carro, aberta for porta. Some adjectives can go before the noun too, sometimes with a change of meaning. This is a common pattern, not a ban on adjectives before nouns.
adjective-after.why: English puts open first; Portuguese says porta [[aberta]], door open.

examples.literal: Has a door open.
The car is open.

contrasts.says: The adjective agrees with its noun whether it is next to it or follows estar.
English normally puts open before door; Portuguese normally puts aberta after porta here.

mistakes.why: aberta agrees with the feminine noun porta.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

progressive.explain: estar plus the -ndo form describes an action in progress: Eu estou andando, I am walking. The estar form follows the subject: eu estou, você está, nós estamos. andando itself stays the same. This is the ordinary Brazilian construction; Portuguese in Portugal also uses estar a with an infinitive.
progressive.why: [[estou andando]] works like am walking: estar carries who and when, while andando names the ongoing action.

examples.text: Eu estou andando para a porta.
examples.literal: I am walking to the door.
We are walking to house.

examples.text: Você está andando para casa também?
examples.literal: You are walking to house too?

contrasts.says: A simple present can describe a habit or, in context, a current action. estar plus -ndo explicitly presents an action in progress.

mistakes.why: With eu, use estou; estamos goes with nós.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.explain: quem asks about a person, o que about a thing or action, onde about a place, and como about a way or a state. Put the question word first in these neutral questions. Portuguese needs no helper like do. Como eu posso ajudar? keeps eu before posso; Onde está o carro? puts the noun after the verb. Other orders are possible in context.
question-word.why: [[Como]] asks how. The rest can keep the statement order: [[eu posso ajudar]]. English puts can before I.

examples.literal: How I can help?

examples.text: Como eu posso ajudar com o café?
examples.means: How can I help with the coffee?
examples.literal: How I can help with the coffee?
How your friend can help?

contrasts.says: Yes-or-no questions ask whether something is true. A question word asks for the missing person, place, thing or way.
How can I help? moves can before I. Como eu posso ajudar? does not have to move the subject.

mistakes.why: A question still needs the eu form posso; podemos belongs with nós.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.explain: Learn ajudar com as a unit when you name the task: ajudar meu amigo com o carro, help my friend with the car. The person helped comes directly after ajudar; com introduces the thing they need help with. Other verbs choose their own patterns. Portuguese does not always use the same preposition as English.
verb-preposition.why: In ajudar meu amigo [[com]] o carro, com links the help to the task.

examples.text: Como eu posso ajudar com o café?
examples.means: How can I help with the coffee?
examples.literal: How I can help with the coffee?

examples.text: Eu estou ajudando meu amigo com o carro.
examples.means: I'm helping my friend with the car.
examples.literal: I am helping my friend with the car.

contrasts.says: A modal introduces a basic verb form, as in posso ajudar. The complement of ajudar then has its own pattern: ajudar com o café.

mistakes.wrong: Eu posso ajudando com o café.
mistakes.right: Eu posso ajudar com o café.
mistakes.why: After posso, use ajudar. ajudando needs a construction such as estou ajudando.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

past.explain: perdi is the completed-past form of perder with eu: Eu perdi sua chave. perdeu is the form with você, ele or ela. It presents the losing as an event that happened. English can say I lost or I have lost when the result matters now; Portuguese does not need a separate have for that single event.
past.why: [[perdi]] carries both I and the completed event. In English the same situation can be [[I have lost]].

examples.literal: I lost your key.

examples.means: Have you lost the key too?
examples.literal: You lost the key too?
I not lost my phone.

contrasts.says: Estou procurando is an ongoing search. Perdi describes the earlier completed event of losing something.

mistakes.why: With eu, the completed-past form is perdi; perdeu goes with você, ele or ela.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: For an event at two, say às duas or às duas horas. hora is feminine, so the number is duas, and it stays feminine when horas is left out. às combines the preposition a and the plural article as. In Minha consulta é às duas, ser gives the time of an event; the ser/estar contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary.
time-telling.why: [[às duas horas]] literally says at the two hours. English says [[at two o'clock]].

examples.text: Eu tenho uma consulta às duas horas.
examples.means: I have an appointment at two o'clock.
examples.literal: I have an appointment at the two hours.

examples.text: Minha consulta é às duas horas.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: My appointment is at the two hours.

examples.text: Nós vamos para casa às duas.
examples.literal: We go to house at the two.

contrasts.says: às is a and as joined, just as na joins em and a.
An event can have its time given with ser: Minha consulta é às duas.

mistakes.wrong: Minha consulta é às dois horas.
mistakes.right: Minha consulta é às duas horas.
mistakes.why: Use feminine duas with feminine horas.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.explain: horas is the plural of hora: two hours are duas horas. Many nouns add -s, though Portuguese also has other plural patterns. In the full agreeing forms taught here, articles, possessives and adjectives match the noun in number and gender. Everyday speech varies in how much plural agreement is pronounced; do not treat every reduced form as impossible Portuguese.
plural.why: The -s in [[horas]] shows more than one. [[duas]] also matches the noun's feminine gender.

examples.text: Eu tenho uma consulta às duas horas.
examples.means: I have an appointment at two o'clock.
examples.literal: I have an appointment at the two hours.

examples.text: O médico vem às duas horas?
examples.means: Is the doctor coming at two o'clock?
examples.literal: The doctor comes at the two hours?

contrasts.says: duas agrees with feminine horas. Number and gender work together.

mistakes.wrong: Eu tenho uma consulta às dois horas.
mistakes.right: Eu tenho uma consulta às duas horas.
mistakes.why: horas is feminine: duas, not masculine dois.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.explain: gostaria is a conditional form of gostar. Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta is a polite way to say I would like to book an appointment. Você gostaria de marcar uma consulta? asks would you like to. This form is the same with eu, você, ele and ela. The conditional has other uses, including hypothetical results, but it is not a replacement for every English would.
conditional.why: [[gostaria de]] makes the request less direct than quero. English expresses that with [[would like to]].

examples.text: Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta.
examples.means: I'd like to book an appointment.
examples.literal: I would like of book an appointment.

examples.text: Você gostaria de marcar uma consulta?
examples.means: Would you like to book an appointment?
examples.literal: You would like of book an appointment?

contrasts.says: The polite gostaria construction keeps de before the requested thing or action.
quero expresses want; gostaria de expresses would like. The degree of politeness and the linking word differ.

mistakes.wrong: Eu gostaria de marcar um consulta.
mistakes.right: Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta.
mistakes.why: The request still needs uma with the feminine noun consulta.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

gostar-de.explain: gostar takes de before what someone likes or would like. Here, gostaria de marcar uma consulta means would like to book an appointment. Keep de before the action as well as before a noun. The ordinary liking forms will use the same connection; unlike English like, gostar selects de.
gostar-de.why: The little word [[de]] belongs to gostar. English says would like to book, while Portuguese says [[gostaria de marcar]].

examples.text: Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta.
examples.means: I'd like to book an appointment.
examples.literal: I would like of book an appointment.

examples.text: Você gostaria de marcar uma consulta?
examples.means: Would you like to book an appointment?
examples.literal: You would like of book an appointment?

contrasts.says: quero marcar has no de. gostaria de marcar keeps the de selected by gostar.

mistakes.why: Before the requested noun, gostar needs de.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

ir-inf.explain: vou, vai or vamos followed by an infinitive can say what is going to happen. In Eu vou pagar por seu café, vou changes with the subject and pagar stays in its basic form. Here it is a plan or offer, not physical movement to a place. English going to is a natural translation.
ir-inf.why: [[vou pagar]] is literally go pay. The unchanged pagar names the planned action.

examples.text: Eu vou pagar por seu café.
examples.means: I'm going to pay for your coffee.
examples.literal: I go pay for your coffee.

contrasts.says: Like posso pagar, vou pagar leaves the second verb in its basic form. vou gives a future plan instead of ability.

mistakes.wrong: Eu vou pago por seu café.
mistakes.right: Eu vou pagar por seu café.
mistakes.why: After vou in this future construction, use pagar, not the eu form pago.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

por-para.explain: English for does not have one Portuguese equivalent. Paying for a thing can be pagar por: Eu vou pagar por seu café. para can introduce a purpose: dinheiro para pagar, money to pay. It also names recipients, as in café para minha mãe. por has other uses, including route and reason; learn each combination in context.
por-para.why: [[por seu café]] names what the payment covers; [[para pagar]] names what the money is for.

examples.text: Eu vou pagar por seu café.
examples.means: I'm going to pay for your coffee.
examples.literal: I go pay for your coffee.

examples.text: Ele não tem dinheiro para pagar.
examples.means: He doesn't have money to pay.
examples.literal: He not has money for pay.
I pay for this book.

contrasts.says: para followed by an infinitive can introduce a purpose.
Both por and para can correspond to for. Choose by the relationship, not by the English word alone.

mistakes.wrong: Eu vou pago por seu café.
mistakes.right: Eu vou pagar por seu café.
mistakes.why: Keep pagar in its basic form after vou; por introduces what is paid for.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-links.explain: An infinitive is a verb's basic form, such as pagar or tomar. Different expressions link to it in different ways: posso pagar has no linking word, gostaria de tomar uses de, and dinheiro para pagar uses para to name a purpose. Do not add or remove a linking word just because English uses to.
infinitive-links.why: [[para pagar]] says the purpose of the money. pagar remains an infinitive, even when the person is ele.

examples.text: Ele não tem dinheiro para pagar.
examples.means: He doesn't have money to pay.
examples.literal: He not has money for pay.

examples.text: Eu gostaria de tomar um café, por favor.
examples.means: I'd like to have a coffee, please.
examples.literal: I would like of drink a coffee, please.

contrasts.says: Modals such as poder can take the infinitive directly: posso pagar.
gostaria keeps de before an infinitive: gostaria de tomar.

mistakes.wrong: Ele não tem dinheiro para pago.
mistakes.right: Ele não tem dinheiro para pagar.
mistakes.why: The purpose is para pagar, with the infinitive, not pago.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

a-gente.explain: a gente is everyday Brazilian we. This path pairs it with the third-person singular verb: A gente faz café, A gente gosta de comer. nós remains a normal alternative, with its own verb forms. In A gente faz café junto, junto is used adverbially for together; it does not identify the group's gender.
a-gente.why: [[A gente]] refers to us, but its verb has the same form as ele's: [[faz]], not the eu form faço.

examples.literal: The people makes coffee together.

examples.text: A gente gosta de comer junto em casa.
examples.means: We like eating together at home.
examples.literal: The people likes of eat together at home.
The people is making coffee.

contrasts.says: você and a gente both use third-person singular verbs here. vocês, plural you, takes third-person plural: vocês fazem.
English we takes make. A gente has singular agreement even though it refers to more than one person.

mistakes.why: faço is the eu form; use faz with a gente in this construction.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: Ligue para o médico is a request or instruction to call the doctor. ligue is the você imperative form selected for this path. Many everyday Brazilian speakers also use liga when addressing você; that is not an inherently wrong form. In a request the listener is understood, so a subject pronoun is normally unnecessary. por favor can soften the request.
imperative.why: [[Ligue]] asks the listener to do something; it does not describe what I or someone else does.

examples.text: Ligue para o médico, por favor.
examples.literal: Call to the doctor, please.

examples.text: Ligue para seu pai, por favor.
examples.literal: Call to your father, please.

contrasts.says: Você pode ligar? asks whether the person can call, often as a request. Ligue directly asks them to call.
por favor can make an instruction gentler; tone matters too.

mistakes.wrong: Ligue para a médico, por favor.
mistakes.right: Ligue para o médico, por favor.
mistakes.why: The instruction still needs the masculine article o with médico.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

softening.explain: por favor can make a request gentler: Ligue para o médico, por favor. Você tem um minuto? is a way to ask whether someone has a little time to listen or help; um minuto need not mean exactly sixty seconds. A question with pode can also function as a request. Tone and context matter, so adding these words does not guarantee politeness.
softening.why: [[um minuto]] presents the request as small. English often says [[a moment]].

examples.text: Ligue para o médico, por favor.
examples.literal: Call to the doctor, please.
You have one minute?

examples.text: Você pode ajudar um minuto, por favor?
examples.means: Can you help for a moment, please?
examples.literal: You can help one minute, please?

contrasts.says: An imperative can be polite with the right phrasing and tone. It is not always a harsh command.

mistakes.why: Use tem with você. tenho belongs with eu.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

ficar.explain: ficar has several related meanings. In Hoje à noite eu fico em casa it means stay: spending the evening at home. In quero ficar sozinha it means be or stay alone. With a place, it can also describe where something is situated. With a description it can express a change of state, so context is needed; it is not just another spelling of estar.
ficar.why: [[fico em casa]] describes staying home. [[estou em casa]] says where I am.

examples.text: Hoje à noite eu fico em casa.
examples.literal: Today at the night I stay at home.

examples.text: Eu quero ficar sozinha hoje à noite.
examples.means: I want to be alone tonight.
examples.literal: I want stay alone today at the night.

examples.text: A gente fica em casa hoje à noite.
examples.literal: The people stays at home today at the night.

contrasts.says: estar can report a current location or state. ficar can add the idea of staying, being situated or becoming, according to context.

mistakes.why: With eu, the form is fico; ficamos goes with nós.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: me identifies the person heard or helped: Você me ouve? te identifies the listener: Eu te ouço. These object pronouns commonly go before the verb in conversational Brazilian Portuguese. With two verbs, Você pode me ouvir? puts me before the infinitive. te with você is normal in much of Brazil. Other placements and other object pronouns occur, especially in formal usage; this is not an all-pronouns-always-first rule.
object-pronoun.why: [[Eu te ouço]] is literally I you hear. English puts the object after the verb: I hear [[you]].

examples.literal: You me hear?
I you hear of new.

examples.means: Can you all hear me too?
examples.literal: You all can me hear too?

contrasts.says: você can be the subject while te refers to the listener as an object. That combination is common Brazilian usage.
In Eu não te ouço, não comes before the pronoun and verb.

mistakes.why: The verb agrees with the subject você, not with me. Use ouve; ouço belongs with eu.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.
